summary: Ukraine is the second-largest country in Europe by area, with fertile black soil that has earned it the name "the breadbasket of Europe"; it became independent from the Soviet Union in 1991 and has been under full-scale Russian invasion since 2022.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: In 988 Grand Prince Volodymyr of Kyivan Rus was baptized under Byzantine influence and ordered the people of Kyiv to be baptized in the Dnieper, and Orthodoxy became the faith of the East Slavic world. In 1686 the Metropolis of Kyiv was placed under the jurisdiction of the Patriarch of Moscow, and during the Soviet period the church suffered severe persecution. In 2019 the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople granted autocephaly (self-governing status) to the "Orthodox Church of Ukraine," and after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 many parishes and believers moved from the Moscow Patriarchate system to the independent Ukrainian church; Orthodoxy remains the largest religion.

ranking.name: Greek Catholicism
ranking.description: In the 1596 Union of Brest, some Orthodox bishops in what was then the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth recognized the authority of the Pope in Rome while retaining the Byzantine rite, forming the Greek Catholic Church. In western Galicia under Austrian rule, this church became the cradle of Ukrainian national consciousness. In 1946 the Soviet Union forced it to merge into the Russian Orthodox Church, and believers operated underground until it was legalized again in 1989, so its followers are concentrated mainly in western regions such as Lviv.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: During 70 years of Soviet rule, atheist education was promoted and large numbers of churches were demolished or closed, and in many families several generations had no religious life. This influence is especially marked in the highly industrialized east and south, which were most deeply shaped by the Soviet system, so people with no religion are found mostly in those regions and in large cities.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: In the 19th century, under the influence of German settler colonists, evangelical movements such as the "Stundists" appeared among peasants in southern Ukraine, and Protestant groups such as the Baptists developed from them. During the Soviet period Protestants suffered severe persecution; after independence in 1991 Western missionary groups entered in large numbers and evangelical churches grew, but their overall numbers remain small.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: The main Muslim adherents are the Crimean Tatars, who converted to Islam during the Crimean Khanate period of the 15th-18th centuries. In 1944 Stalin deported them all to Central Asia on charges of collaboration, and they returned home only gradually after 1989; after Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014, many were again persecuted or forced to leave.

religion.background: In 988 Kyivan Rus accepted Orthodoxy, and Kyiv became the cradle of East Slavic Christianity. After the Middle Ages, Ukraine was divided among different powers: the west developed Greek Catholicism under Polish and Austrian rule, while the Crimean Khanate in the south followed Islam. Religion was harshly suppressed during the Soviet period, and revived after independence in 1991. In 2019 the Orthodox Church of Ukraine obtained autocephaly, and after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 the question of church affiliation became an important issue of national identity.

language.official: Ukrainian is the sole official language.

ranking.name: Ukrainian
ranking.description: Ukrainian belongs to the East Slavic branch and derives from the Old East Slavic of the Kyivan Rus period. In the Russian Empire, the 1863 Valuev Circular and the 1876 Ems Ukaz banned publications in Ukrainian, and during the Soviet period Russification was long pursued. In 1989 Ukrainian became the state language, and the 2019 Language Law strengthened its public status; Russian aggression in 2014 and 2022 also led many formerly Russian-speaking people to switch to Ukrainian, and its share of use keeps rising.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: The spread of Russian stems from centuries of rule by the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union; in the Soviet period Russian was the main language of administration, higher education and urban life. The eastern industrial region of the Donbas absorbed large numbers of Russian migrants in the 20th century, and the south and the large cities are also predominantly Russian-speaking. After 2014, and especially after the outbreak of full-scale war in 2022, many Ukrainians have reduced their use of Russian for political and identity reasons, and its share has fallen markedly.

ranking.name: Crimean Tatar
ranking.description: Crimean Tatar belongs to the Turkic family and was the language of the Crimean Khanate founded in the 15th century. In 1944 Stalin deported all the Crimean Tatars to Central Asia, and the language suffered severe loss in exile; its revival began only after the people returned home after 1989. After Russia occupied Crimea in 2014, Tatar-language education and media were again curtailed.

language.history: Ukrainian derives from the East Slavic of the Kyivan Rus period and, under Polish-Lithuanian rule in the 14th-17th centuries, absorbed a good deal of Polish vocabulary. Ivan Kotliarevsky's Eneida (Aeneid), written in 1798 in the popular spoken language, is regarded as the beginning of modern Ukrainian literature, and in the 19th century the poet Taras Shevchenko established the standing of the national literature. The Russian Empire and the Soviet Union long suppressed Ukrainian; after independence in 1991 it became the only official language, and in recent years the war has strengthened its standing as a symbol of national identity.

ranking.name: Borscht
ranking.description: A red soup based on beetroot, simmered with cabbage, potatoes, carrots and pork or beef, served with a spoonful of sour cream and often accompanied by garlic bread.
ranking.history: The name borscht is believed to come from "hogweed" (borshchevyk), a plant anciently used to make soup, which beetroot later replaced as the source of the soup's color. There are dozens of different versions across Ukraine, each family has its own inherited recipe, and borscht appears on the tables at weddings, funerals and holidays. During Russia's invasion in 2022, "Culture of Ukrainian borscht cooking" was inscribed by UNESCO on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding, becoming a symbol of cultural identity.

ranking.name: Varenyky
ranking.description: Dough wrappers are filled with mashed potato, farmer's cheese, sauerkraut or sour cherries, boiled, and topped with butter, sour cream or fried onions; both sweet and savory versions exist.
ranking.history: The name varenyky comes from the Ukrainian word for "to boil" (varyty); it is generally believed to be related to dumpling traditions of Central Asia and the Turkic peoples, passing to Eastern Europe through exchange among steppe peoples. In the 19th century the writer Gogol described Cossacks feasting on varenyky in his stories, making it a symbol of Ukrainian national character. At the Christmas Eve "Twelve Meatless Dishes" supper, varenyky filled with potato or sauerkraut are one of the essential dishes.

ranking.name: Holubtsi (cabbage rolls)
ranking.description: Blanched cabbage leaves are wrapped around rice and ground meat or vegetables, arranged in a pot and stewed in tomato sauce until tender, and eaten with sour cream.
ranking.history: Cabbage rolls resemble the Ottoman tradition of "dolma" (stuffed dishes) and are generally believed to have come to Eastern Europe through contact with the Ottomans and Crimean Tatars, with locally easy-to-store cabbage replacing grape leaves. The name "holubtsi" means "little doves," describing the shape of the rolls. It is a labor-intensive dish common at Christmas, weddings and family gatherings, and the fillings vary from region to region.

ranking.name: Salo (cured pork fatback)
ranking.description: Pork back fat is cured with salt, garlic and spices and aged, then sliced thinly and eaten with rye bread, garlic or onion; it can also be smoked or used for frying.
ranking.history: In cold Eastern Europe, where food supplies were unstable, salo was a long-keeping, high-calorie food greatly valued by peasants and Cossacks. One popular claim holds that the Ottomans and Crimean Tatars did not plunder pork during raids, so raising pigs became a way to protect food supplies, but this is hard to verify. Today salo is regarded as a representative Ukrainian food, places such as Lviv even hold salo festivals, and Ukrainians often joke about it themselves.

ranking.name: Chicken Kyiv
ranking.description: A chicken breast is pounded thin, wrapped around chilled herb butter, rolled, coated in breadcrumbs and deep-fried; when cut open, the melted butter flows out.
ranking.history: This dish derives from French cuisine fashionable among the nobility of the Russian Empire in the 18th-19th centuries and developed from the chicken cutlets of French cooking. In the Soviet period of the 20th century it became the signature dish of upscale Kyiv restaurants and hotels, and spread to the West under the name "Kyiv," becoming very popular in restaurants in the United States and Britain as well. Today it is regarded as a representative dish of the Ukrainian capital and also reflects the historical traces of the imperial-era aristocratic cuisine.
